chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Prince Robinson and Ed Inge on clarinet
summary: Prince Robinson played the clarinet solos on McKinney's early records; Ed Inge played a very modern clarinet, years ahead, and could arrange.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Let's go on to some of the saxophone players. We've mentioned Hilton Jefferson. Of course we've got the Pres Dupreys, Coleman Hawkins.
And, of course, Prince Robinson Robertson.
Yeah. He was a fantastic clarinet player and a good tenor player back in those days. He was with McKinney Cottonpickers.
Oh, he first played with McKinney also, huh?

Oh, sure. Yeah, he played all the clarinet solos on the first record until later, about the last, oh, I'll say 1932, Edward Inge played some of the clarinet solos, you see. A very good saxophone player.
And, of course, we named Bennie Carter and, of

Ed Inge was a very good clarinet player, a very good clarinet player. He played the most modern clarinet that I've ever heard. He played clarinet back in the thirties like Bird played alto in the forties.

He was that far ahead. And the guys used to listen to him and say, 'What is he playing?' you know, but he was all over the clarinet. And if you tried to follow him in a passage like a guy would be repetitious, he was never repetitious.
If you tried to follow him down the line, he'd turn left on you, you know.
That's the way he played, and he would write the same way.
Oh, he was an arranger also, huh?
